page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: The Boyle temperature of a gas is the
temperature at which a real gas obeys the ideal
gas laws over an appreciable range of pressure.
At this temperature Z ≈ 1, because the attraction
and volume corrections cancel each other.
steps.why: A real gas deviates below ideal at some temperatures and above at others; at one temperature in between, the two deviations balance and the gas behaves ideally over a wide pressure range. That balancing temperature is named after Boyle.
common_mistakes: Saying the gas becomes ideal at ALL pressures. The ideal behaviour holds over a range of pressure, not everywhere.
Confusing Boyle temperature with critical temperature. They are different quantities.
steps.memory_tip: The temperature where a REAL gas behaves like Boyle's IDEAL gas — hence the name.
steps.margin_note: Real gas, ideal behaviour, range of pressure: those three pieces make the definition.

steps.label: The expression
lines: where a and b are the van der Waals constants
of the gas and R is the gas constant.
Each gas has its own Boyle temperature, since
a and b differ from gas to gas.
steps.why: The Boyle temperature comes from the van der Waals constants: a measures attraction and b measures molecular volume, and their ratio a/(Rb) is the temperature where the two corrections cancel.
common_mistakes: Treating the Boyle temperature as universal. It is different for each gas because a and b are.
steps.memory_tip: Attraction over volume: a on top, R times b below.
steps.margin_note: Defining a and b as the van der Waals constants completes the expression.

insider_note: The unstarred tail of this chapter still turns up in papers — this one is a two-line answer, and the expression a/(Rb) is the half most scripts leave out.
